1.goal: To name the scene and say that this lesson closes the block.
1.interaction: T–S, one open question after you set the scene.
run: Tell him this is the last of the four and that it puts the other three together: reading two versions (9), holding a turn at someone else's speed (10), arguing in hypotheticals under objection (11).
Say that this is the scene he is training for — his profile records international travel in July, and this is the conversation he will have there.
1.expected: That everything he can take for granted with a Brazilian colleague has to be said, or the argument does not mean what he thinks it means.
1.support: If the answer stays general, ask what she would assume about his role if he did not tell her the defense is assigned.
1.challenge: Ask which single fact about the system, left out, would break the argument fastest.
1.monitoring: Whether he frames the difficulty as language or as shared knowledge. It is the second, and the lesson is built on that.
1.evidence: What he names as changing when the listener is outside the system.
1.transition: Move on when he has said what changes when the other person does not know the system he works in.

2.goal: To see how he explains it BEFORE any guidance.
2.interaction: S talks for three minutes; you time it and say nothing.
run: Give the instruction below and start the clock.
Do not interrupt, do not steer, and time it for real.
If he runs over, let him, and write down by how much. It is data, not a fault.
exact: Tell me your position on this case — starting now.
2.expected: Whatever he has. Very likely: more background than the three minutes hold.
2.support: None here. Anything you add contaminates the baseline this screen exists to take.
2.challenge: None here, for the same reason.
2.monitoring: What he explains without being asked, and what he assumes she already knows. Note the point at which the background explanation ends — that number is what round 2 is compared against.
2.evidence: Where the background ended, and how long the whole thing ran. Both are the comparison for stage 8.
2.transition: Move on when he stops on his own, or at four minutes.

3.goal: To hear the three things she does: a clarifying question, a reformulation of what she understood, and the objection of substance.
3.interaction: S listens, then T–S on the two questions.
run: Read the two questions WITH him before you play.
Play once. The transcript opens afterwards.
3.expected: The third one is the real objection — “if the delay explains them, it explains them for both sides”. The other two are her catching up. And yes, the objection is correct: that is why denying it is expensive.
3.support: If he treats all three as objections, play the first one again and ask what she is asking for — information, or a change of position.
3.challenge: Ask which of the three he would find hardest to answer in sixty seconds.
3.monitoring: Whether he accepts that she is right. Everything in stages 4 and 5 depends on granting it — a student who decides the objection is wrong will spend round 1 defending instead of answering.
3.evidence: Whether he grants the objection here, before any pressure. It predicts what happens at stage 6.
3.transition: Move on when he recognizes that the objection holds.

4.goal: To decide what goes into the three minutes and what stays out.
4.interaction: S classifies alone, then T–S against his own attempt at stage 2.
run: He classifies the six, then Check — the wrong lines show what they were and the explanation opens.
Then compare with his own attempt at stage 2: which of the things he said would sit in the middle column?
exact: “We are assigned to the case” — if she does not know that, does your argument mean something different? (Yes: she will assume the family hired him, and that strategy was a choice.)
4.expected: She needs it now: the jury decides guilt and not the sentence · we are assigned, the family does not choose us · the statement came eleven days late. It costs you time: the year the court was built. Later, if she asks: his eleven years of jury work · the caseload.
4.support: If the sorting is by interest rather than by need, go back to the CCQ and apply it to each line in turn.
4.challenge: Ask what he would add to the first column if she were a judge instead of a lawyer.
4.monitoring: Whether the criterion he arrives at is about her, or about the material. Only the first survives contact with a real listener.
4.evidence: How much of his stage-2 attempt he himself puts in the middle column.
4.transition: Move on when he names the criterion — not “is it interesting?” but “does my argument mean something different if she does not know it?”

5.goal: The answer to the objection, isolated, before the simulation.
5.interaction: S marks on screen, then writes one sentence and reads it out loud.
run: He marks the two that work, the explanation opens, and then he writes the opening line — one sentence, in the field on screen.
This is the only writing in the lesson, and it is the first writing sample of the cycle — the skills profile records writing as not yet observed. One sentence is enough to change that.
Then he reads it aloud once and puts it away. He will not have it in front of him in the simulation.
5.expected: The two that work: “That is fair — it does cut both ways. The difference is who had to prove it that night” and “It does, and that is exactly why the burden matters”. Going back to the beginning is a restart, and flat denial spends the credit she gave him.
5.support: If the sentence comes out as a denial, ask what he is granting in it. If the answer is nothing, it is a denial.
5.challenge: Ask for a second version of the same sentence, shorter, and which of the two he would rather have in the room.
5.monitoring: Whether the concession and the turn are both in the sentence, or only the concession.
5.evidence: The written sentence itself — the first writing sample of the cycle. Keep it.
5.transition: Move on when the sentence is written and said.

6.goal: The product of the block: the position explained to someone outside the system, with one objection of substance absorbed without starting over.
6.interaction: Role-play. You are Claire; you interrupt once and then stop talking.
run: Let it run for about ninety seconds, then make the objection — the “cuts both ways” one — and stop talking.
ONE objection, and of substance. Not three small ones: three interruptions turn it into a conversation, and then the lesson is no longer measuring whether he can hold a line.
If he goes back to the beginning, let him. That is exactly what stage 7 gives back.
No paper, no case on screen. Close everything before he starts.
exact: If the delay explains the inconsistencies, it explains them for both sides.
6.expected: The objection granted, then answered, without restarting the explanation.
6.support: If he stalls after the objection, wait. The silence is his to use, and filling it removes the measurement.
6.challenge: None during the round. Everything extra goes to round 2.
6.monitoring: Whether he grants the objection before answering · whether the hypothetical form from lesson 11 appears inside the argument, unprompted · where the background explanation ends.
6.evidence: What he did at the objection — granted, denied, or restarted — and whether the hypothetical form appeared on its own.
6.transition: Move on when he closes, or at five minutes.

7.goal: To give back what happened in round 1, in the three terms that round 2 will test.
7.interaction: T–S, filling the three fields together.
run: Fill the fields on screen with him. THREE points here, not two — this is the lesson that closes the block, and the feedback feeds the record: (1) what she needed and did not get; (2) what cost time and did not need to be there; (3) what happened at the objection — granted, denied, or restarted.
Then announce round 2: sixty seconds, same position, and she already knows how the system works.
Teach nothing new here. The upgrade is about what has already happened.
7.expected: Three points he recognizes, at least one of them about time spent rather than about language.
7.support: If he cannot say what she needed and did not get, read back the first thirty seconds of his round 1 and ask what she could do with it.
7.challenge: Ask him to say, before round 2, which of the three he intends to fix.
7.monitoring: Whether the point about the objection is one he can state himself. If he cannot, he did not notice what he did.
7.evidence: The three fields. They are the input for the record and for the route of block 2.
7.transition: Move on when the three points are on the board and round 2 has been announced.

8.goal: The same position in sixty seconds, with the context already given.
8.interaction: Role-play, round 2. You are Claire, and you make the same objection in the same place.
run: Time it.
Make the SAME objection, in the same place.
If the hypothetical form from lesson 11 appears here, inside the argument and unprompted, write down the exact sentence: it answers the first of the two open points in the profile.
exact: If the delay explains the inconsistencies, it explains them for both sides.
8.expected: The same position in a third of the time, with the background gone and the argument intact.
8.support: If he cannot cut, ask what Claire already knows. The answer removes half of it.
8.challenge: Ask for it once more in thirty seconds, and see what survives twice.
8.monitoring: What he CUTS when the time drops to a third and the background is already known. Cutting the explanation means he read his listener. Cutting the argument in order to keep the explanation means he did not.
8.evidence: What he cut, and the exact sentence if the hypothetical form appeared unprompted.
8.transition: Move on when the sixty seconds are up.

9.goal: To close the block: the four lessons read together, as the input for planning 13–28.
9.interaction: T–S over the four lessons; the reading is yours to record, not to negotiate.
run: Read the four lines on screen with him.
Do not decide the route now. Record and close — the route is decided with the four records in hand, not in the last minute of the lesson.
9.expected: Recognition of the four operations as one line of work, rather than four separate lessons.
9.support: If the four read as unrelated, name the thread out loud: a claim, its source, its limits, and holding it against someone.
9.challenge: Ask which of the four he would want more of, and hold the answer for the planning — without promising it.
9.monitoring: Whether he sees the block as one arc. The answer belongs in the record either way.
9.evidence: Open point 1 — did the hypothetical form appear on its own, inside the argument? Write the exact sentence. Open point 2 — did the B1+ hold with a subject and an interlocutor he did not choose? And the three first isolated samples of the cycle: reading (lesson 9), listening (lesson 10) and writing (the sentence from stage 5). The skills profile was empty in all three.
9.transition: Move on when the four are recorded.

10.goal: To register the lesson and close the block with the next step named, but not promised.
10.interaction: S ticks the list and answers the scale; T–S on the close.
run: Read the list with him. The confidence row is his.

Homework, said out loud and never put on screen: the post-class has the ninety-second recording — the July scene — and the longest piece of writing in the block. Plus two videos: Melissa Marshall on explaining technical work to people outside it, and Adichie.
Next block: it depends on the lesson that closes the block. Do NOT promise a topic.
10.expected: One phrase named as usable, and one honest answer on the confidence row.
10.support: If nothing is named, ask which sentence he would take into the July conversation.
10.challenge: Ask what he would want the first lesson of the next block to be, and record it without agreeing to it.
10.monitoring: Whether the confidence reading matches what round 2 showed. A gap either way is worth recording.
10.evidence: Fill the post-lesson record now, while the lesson is fresh. It is the main evidence for reading the four together.
10.transition: Close the lesson, and the block.
